- Verbatim Textbook Definitions:
- Electric Current: "The amount of charge flowing through a particular area in unit time (rate of flow of electric charges)." [SI Unit: Ampere (A) or C/s]
- Electric Circuit: "A continuous and closed path of an electric current." [SI Unit: N/A]

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:
  - In-Text Exercises (Page 172):
    * [Q1] (conceptual): What does an electric circuit mean?
      Method: Define electric circuit as a continuous and closed path of an electric current.
    * [Q2] (conceptual): Define the unit of current.
      Method: Define 1 Ampere as 1 coulomb of charge flowing per second.
    * [Q3] (numerical): Calculate the number of electrons constituting one coulomb of charge.
      Method: Use n = Q/e where Q = 1 C and e = 1.6 * 10^-19 C to get 6.25 * 10^18 electrons.

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Electric Current ($I = Q/t$)":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): What is the SI unit of electric current?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Ampere (A)
      -> Socratic Hint: Think of the French scientist Andre-Marie Ampere after whom it is named.
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): Define 1 ampere of electric current.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: 1 ampere is constituted by the flow of one coulomb of charge per second (1 A = 1 C/1 s).
      -> Socratic Hint: Relate current I = Q/t with Q = 1 C and t = 1 s.
    * [Q3] (3-mark Derivation): Calculate the amount of charge flowing through a conductor if a current of 0.5 A flows for 10 minutes.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Given I = 0.5 A, t = 10 min = 600 s. Q = I * t = 0.5 * 600 = 300 C.
      -> Socratic Hint: Convert minutes into seconds before multiplying with current.
    * [Q4] (5-mark Numerical): A current of 2 A flows through a conductor for 5 minutes. Find (a) total charge passing through cross-section, (b) total number of electrons flowing.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: (a) Q = I * t = 2 * 300 = 600 C. (b) n = Q/e = 600 / (1.6 * 10^-19) = 3.75 * 10^21 electrons.
      -> Socratic Hint: Use Q = ne where charge of electron e = 1.6 * 10^-19 C.
    * [Q5] (PYQ): State the relationship between electric current, charge, and time. Write its SI unit.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: I = Q/t. SI unit of electric current is Ampere (A).
      -> Socratic Hint: Recall the basic definition: rate of flow of electric charges.
    * [Q6] (Competency): Why is an ammeter always connected in series in an electric circuit?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: An ammeter has very low resistance and measures the entire current flowing through that part of the circuit.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think about whether a current measuring device needs to experience the full flow of charge.
  * Concept #2 "Quantization of Charge ($Q = ne$)":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): How many electrons constitute one coulomb of charge?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Nearly 6 * 10^18 electrons.
      -> Socratic Hint: Divide 1 C by the charge of a single electron (1.6 * 10^-19 C).
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): What is the magnitude of charge on an electron?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: An electron possesses a negative charge of 1.6 * 10^-19 C.
      -> Socratic Hint: Memorize fundamental elementary charge value.
    * [Q3] (3-mark Derivation): Verify that 1 C of charge contains 6.25 * 10^18 electrons.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: n = 1 / (1.6 * 10^-19) = 6.25 * 10^18 electrons.
      -> Socratic Hint: Perform division 1 / 1.6 and adjust exponent.
    * [Q4] (5-mark Numerical): Calculate the total charge on 10^20 electrons.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Q = ne = 10^20 * 1.6 * 10^-19 C = 16 C.
      -> Socratic Hint: Multiply number of electrons n by charge e.
    * [Q5] (PYQ): Calculate the number of electrons constituting one coulomb of charge.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: n = Q/e = 1 / (1.6 * 10^-19) = 6.25 * 10^18 electrons.
      -> Socratic Hint: Direct NCERT in-text question solution.
    * [Q6] (Competency): Can a charge of 3.2 * 10^-19 C exist on a body? Explain.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Yes, because it is an integral multiple of elementary charge (n = 3.2 * 10^-19 / 1.6 * 10^-19 = 2).
      -> Socratic Hint: Check if Q/e results in an integer.

chapter_notes: Electricity is a controllable and convenient form of energy. A continuous and closed path of an electric current is called an electric circuit. Electric current is expressed as the rate of flow of electric charges ($I = Q/t$). In metallic wires, electrons constitute the flow of charges. Conventionally, the direction of electric current is taken as opposite to the direction of the flow of electrons. The SI unit of electric charge is coulomb (C), equivalent to 6 * 10^18 electrons. The SI unit of current is ampere (A). An ammeter measures electric current and is always connected in series.

ai_system_prompt_context:
CBSE Class 10 Science Module 2: Electric Potential and Potential Difference. Final-Term Examination Syllabus. Use the water pump and tank analogy to explain potential difference clearly.
TEXTBOOK GROUNDING & MANDATORY TEACHING DIRECTIVES (PHASE 5 20-MINUTE MASTER CLASS):
- Capsule Duration: 20 Minutes (Full comprehensive lesson covering all textbook nuances)
- Capsule Overview Diagram: A resistor connected in a circuit with a voltmeter bridging across its two ends (parallel branch).
- Diagram Type: circuit_schematic
- Chapter Multi-Level Flowchart: Chemical Energy in Cell -> Potential Difference (V = W/Q) -> Electric Pressure -> Charge Motion
- FLOWCHART DIRECTIVE: Call write_chalkboard(action="draw_flowchart", content="Chemical Energy in Cell -> Potential Difference (V = W/Q) -> Electric Pressure -> Charge Motion") to visually organize the concepts on the board!

- Verbatim Textbook Definitions:
- Potential Difference: "Work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other in an electric circuit." [SI Unit: Volt (V) or J C^-1]

- Textbook Concrete Examples:
- Water tank pressure analogy: Water flows out of a tube when connected to a tank kept at a higher level, creating pressure difference.

- AUTHENTIC TEXTBOOK EXERCISES & QUESTIONS:
  - In-Text Exercises (Page 174):
    * [Q1] (conceptual): Name a device that helps to maintain a potential difference across a conductor.
      Method: A cell or battery.
    * [Q2] (conceptual): What is meant by saying that the potential difference between two points is 1 V?
      Method: 1 joule of work is done to move 1 coulomb of charge between the points.
    * [Q3] (numerical): How much energy is given to each coulomb of charge passing through a 6 V battery?
      Method: Energy (Work) = V * Q = 6 V * 1 C = 6 J.

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Potential Difference ($V = W/Q$)":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): What is the SI unit of electric potential difference?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Volt (V)
      -> Socratic Hint: Named after Italian physicist Alessandro Volta.
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): Define 1 volt of potential difference.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: 1 volt is the potential difference between two points when 1 joule of work is done to move a charge of 1 coulomb from one point to the other.
      -> Socratic Hint: V = W/Q where W = 1 J and Q = 1 C.
    * [Q3] (3-mark Derivation): How much work is done in moving a charge of 2 C across two points having potential difference 12 V?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: W = V * Q = 12 V * 2 C = 24 J.
      -> Socratic Hint: Rearrange V = W/Q to W = VQ.
    * [Q4] (5-mark Numerical): Calculate the work done in moving a charge of 5 C from a point at 115 V to a point at 120 V.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Potential difference V = 120 - 115 = 5 V. Work W = V * Q = 5 V * 5 C = 25 J.
      -> Socratic Hint: Find the difference in potential first.
    * [Q5] (PYQ): Name the device used to measure potential difference across a conductor and state how it is connected in a circuit.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Voltmeter; it is always connected in parallel across the points.
      -> Socratic Hint: Contrast with ammeter which is in series.
    * [Q6] (Competency): Why does water flow from a high tank to a lower one? How does this relate to electric charges flowing in a wire?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Water flows due to pressure difference. Similarly, electrons flow only when there is an electric pressure difference (potential difference) maintained by a cell or battery.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think of the pressure difference water analogy in the textbook.

- CONCEPT-BY-CONCEPT VISUAL PLAYBOOK (MANDATORY UNIQUE DRAWINGS):
  * Concept #1 "Potential Difference ($V = W/Q$)":
    - Visual Title: "Voltmeter in Parallel Setup" (circuit_schematic)
    - Why Needed: Illustrates how a voltmeter bridges across a component without breaking the main line.

chapter_notes: Georg Simon Ohm found that potential difference V is directly proportional to current I ($V = IR$). The constant R is resistance, measured in ohms (\Omega). Resistance depends directly on length ($l$) and inversely on area of cross-section ($A$), and on material nature: $R = \rho \frac{l}{A}$, where $\rho$ is electrical resistivity. Metals have very low resistivity, while insulators have extremely high resistivity. Alloys are used in heating devices due to high resistivity and resistance to oxidation.

      -> Ideal Model Answer: V = V1 + V2 + V3. By Ohm's law, IRs = IR1 + IR2 + IR3. Canceling I gives Rs = R1 + R2 + R3.

    * [Q2] (numerical): Compute heat generated while transferring 96,000 C of charge in 1 hour through 50 V potential difference.
      Method: H = V * Q = 50 V * 96000 C = 4.8 * 10^6 J.

- PREPARED 4-6 EXAM-AUTHENTIC QUESTIONS PER CONCEPT:
  * Concept #1 "Joule's Law of Heating ($H = I^2Rt$)":
    * [Q1] (1-mark MCQ): What is the SI unit of heat energy?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Joule (J)
      -> Socratic Hint: Standard work/energy unit.
    * [Q2] (2-mark Definition): State Joule's Law of Heating.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Heat produced in a resistor is (i) directly proportional to square of current ($I^2$), (ii) directly proportional to resistance ($R$), and (iii) directly proportional to time ($t$).
      -> Socratic Hint: H = I^2 * R * t.
    * [Q3] (3-mark Derivation): Derive Joule's heating formula $H = I^2Rt$.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: Work done $W = VQ$. Since $Q = It$ and $V = IR$, substituting gives $W = (IR)(It)t$ -> $H = I^2Rt$.
      -> Socratic Hint: Combine VQ and Ohm's law.
    * [Q4] (5-mark Numerical): 100 J of heat is produced each second in a 4 \Omega resistance. Find potential difference across resistor.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: H/t = 100 J/s, R = 4 \Omega. I = \sqrt{H / (Rt)} = \sqrt{100 / 4} = 5 A. V = IR = 5 * 4 = 20 V.
      -> Socratic Hint: Find current using H = I^2Rt, then calculate V = IR.
    * [Q5] (PYQ): Why does the cord of an electric heater not glow while the heating element does?
      -> Ideal Model Answer: The heating element has very high resistance compared to the connecting cord, so much more heat is dissipated in the element causing it to glow.
      -> Socratic Hint: Compare resistances using H = I^2Rt.
    * [Q6] (Competency): Explain how an electric fuse protects home appliances during a short circuit.
      -> Ideal Model Answer: A fuse wire has low melting point and is connected in series. When current exceeds safe limit, excess heat melts the fuse wire, breaking the circuit.
      -> Socratic Hint: Think of current surge and melting point.

      -> Ideal Model Answer: Kilowatt-hour (kWh) or 'unit'
      -> Socratic Hint: Power in kW multiplied by hours.

questions.question: State Joule's Law of Heating.
questions.ideal_answer: Heat produced in a resistor is (i) directly proportional to square of current ($I^2$), (ii) directly proportional to resistance ($R$), and (iii) directly proportional to time ($t$).
questions.socratic_hint: H = I^2 * R * t.

questions.question: Derive Joule's heating formula $H = I^2Rt$.
questions.ideal_answer: Work done $W = VQ$. Since $Q = It$ and $V = IR$, substituting gives $W = (IR)(It)t$ -> $H = I^2Rt$.
questions.socratic_hint: Combine VQ and Ohm's law.

questions.question: 100 J of heat is produced each second in a 4 \Omega resistance. Find potential difference across resistor.
questions.ideal_answer: H/t = 100 J/s, R = 4 \Omega. I = \sqrt{H / (Rt)} = \sqrt{100 / 4} = 5 A. V = IR = 5 * 4 = 20 V.
questions.socratic_hint: Find current using H = I^2Rt, then calculate V = IR.

questions.question: Why does the cord of an electric heater not glow while the heating element does?

worked_examples.problem: In-Text Question (Section 11.5, p. 15): How can three resistors of resistances 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 6 Ω be connected to give a total resistance of: (a) 4 Ω, (b) 1 Ω?
worked_examples.substitution:
(a) Parallel combination of 3 Ω and 6 Ω in series with 2 Ω.
(b) All three resistors in parallel.
worked_examples.calculation:
1. Case (a): Connect 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel:
   $R_p = \frac{3 \times 6}{3 + 6} = \frac{18}{9} = 2\,\Omega$.
   Connect this combination in series with the 2 Ω resistor:
   $R_{\text{total}} = 2\,\Omega + R_p = 2 + 2 = 4\,\Omega$.
2. Case (b): Connect all three resistors in parallel:
   $\frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{6} = \frac{3 + 2 + 1}{6} = \frac{6}{6} = 1\,\Omega \implies R_p = 1\,\Omega$.
worked_examples.finalAnswer: (a) Connect 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel, then in series with 2 Ω (total 4 Ω); (b) Connect all three resistors in parallel (total 1 Ω).

questions.question: A wire of resistance R is cut into 5 equal parts and connected in parallel to give R'. Ratio R/R' is:
questions.socratic_hint: Each piece has resistance R/5. In parallel, 1/R' = 5/(R/5) + ... = 25/R -> R/R' = 25.

questions.question: Which of the following does not represent electrical power? (a) I^2R, (b) IR^2, (c) VI, (d) V^2/R
questions.ideal_answer: (b) IR^2 because P = VI = (IR)I = I^2R = V(V/R) = V^2/R.
questions.socratic_hint: Substitute Ohm's law into P = VI.

questions.question: A copper wire has diameter 0.5 mm and resistivity 1.6 * 10^-8 \Omega m. What will be length to make resistance 10 \Omega? How much does resistance change if diameter is doubled?
questions.ideal_answer: l = RA / \rho = (10 * \pi * (0.25 * 10^-3)^2) / (1.6 * 10^-8) = 122.7 m. If diameter doubles, area becomes 4 times, so resistance becomes 1/4th (2.5 \Omega).
questions.socratic_hint: R is inversely proportional to d^2.

questions.question: Show how you would connect three resistors of 6 \Omega each to get total resistance of (i) 9 \Omega, (ii) 4 \Omega.
questions.ideal_answer: (i) Connect two in parallel (giving 3 \Omega) in series with the third (3 + 6 = 9 \Omega). (ii) Connect two in series (giving 12 \Omega) in parallel with the third (12 * 6 / 18 = 4 \Omega).
questions.socratic_hint: Test series/parallel combinations of 6 \Omega.

questions.question: Several bulbs designed for 220 V are rated 10 W. How many can be connected in parallel on a 220 V line if max current is 5 A?
questions.ideal_answer: Current per bulb = P/V = 10 / 220 = 1/22 A. Total current = 5 A. Number of bulbs = 5 / (1/22) = 110 bulbs.
questions.socratic_hint: Divide max allowable current by current per bulb.
